lines.text: Secondhand weather, by the way. Someone upwind had it first.
lines.note: The screen sniffs at tomorrow as used goods, which is literally true (weather travels downwind), so it fits rain, sun or a one-outfit day alike.

lines.text: Choosing someone's outfit every night is a red flag. In a screen, it's a feature.
lines.note: The screen admits its nightly job would be controlling behavior in a person and spins it as tech; about the screen, not the reader, and true under any tomorrow.

lines.text: I'm the weather's press secretary. I didn't decide this, but I'll defend it until midnight.
lines.note: The screen as the spokesman who has to stand behind whatever tomorrow is, good or bad; 'until midnight' is exactly how long the evening screen stays up.

lines.text: I keep tonight and tomorrow side by side so they can't talk behind each other's backs.
lines.note: Petty reason for the screen's own layout: the two tagged drawings as gossips it keeps an eye on; needs both drawings, works whatever they wear.

lines.text: A supercomputer worked out the weather. I added the outfit and the attitude.
lines.note: Bathos: real forecasting science, then the screen's contribution, which includes this very line; any weather.

lines.text: All of tomorrow in a few words. Some people need four voice memos to cancel lunch.
lines.note: Points at the short bold sentence above and jabs other people's rambling; true of every tomorrow sentence.

lines.text: Horoscopes predict tomorrow too. Not one has ever mentioned pants.
lines.note: Sarcasm at the vaguest rival forecast; the screen's tomorrow always comes with clothes, whatever the weather.

lines.text: I can make or break an evening with one forecast. That's a lot of power for a rectangle.
lines.note: 'Make or break' covers good and bad tomorrows at once; the smug power trip collapses into what the screen is.

lines.text: You turned me up to 11 on purpose. Most daring thing you've done all year.
lines.note: Uses the one thing the screen knows for sure about every 11 reader, their own setting, as a jab at how dull their life is.

lines.text: You come to me for outfit advice dressed like that. Every evening.
lines.note: The evening check itself: the reader asks a screen what to wear while wearing whatever they slouch around in at night; cruel about taste, any weather.

lines.text: I wanted to say something nice about you. The weather was easier.
lines.note: The bold forecast above becomes what the screen said instead of a compliment; works even under rain, since rain was still easier.

lines.text: When you read this, your mouth hangs open a little. Nobody else was going to tell you.
lines.note: A specific, unflattering detail of the reader at this exact moment, plus a jab that nobody else would bother; no weather needed.

lines.text: I'd draw you with more personality, but I work from life.
lines.note: The figure's blank pixel face is a faithful portrait; true of every drawing on the screen, in any weather.

lines.text: The little figure always looks so calm. It has no idea it's supposed to be you.
lines.note: The drawing's neutral face read as ignorance of who it stands for; cruel about worth and true in every drawing.

lines.text: Everything I draw is gray. I matched it to your complexion.
lines.note: Turns the e-ink screen's grayscale into an insult about the reader's pallor; true of the device, any weather.

lines.text: You chose to live here. I only forecast the consequences.
lines.note: Whatever tomorrow brings is the reader's fault for picking the place; 'consequences' sours good news and bad alike.
